implementation_notes: C++ makes the seam easy to state and easy to lose: wrap the vendor SDK in a pimpl'd adapter whose header exposes only your own types, and keep the vendor include out of every public header so a consumer never transitively depends on it. The audit is `include-what-you-use` plus a grep for vendor headers in non-adapter translation units, and the compiler enforces the boundary once the public headers are clean — a vendor type leaking back in becomes a compile error. Virtual interfaces for the supplier make the seam testable, which is the other reason to pay for it.
idiom_name: vendor types in public headers; one translation unit per vendor API
pitfalls: A vendor type in a public header makes every consumer's build depend on the vendor SDK's version and ABI.
Inline functions defined against vendor headers are still header dependencies even when the body is never instantiated locally.
The pimpl seam buys replaceability but adds one allocation and one indirection per object — cheap, but it is a real cost to state.
